cards.title: Post-Purchase Survey Questions Worth Copying
cards.summary: Post-purchase surveys can reveal acquisition source, timing, competitive set, and even who to book next as an influencer.
cards.use_when: Building or refreshing a post-purchase survey on Shopify to inform creative, media mix, and influencer booking decisions.

cards.title: YouTube Influencer Strategy: Patience and Portfolio Math
cards.summary: YouTube influencer ad reads are a venture-style portfolio play that requires deep payback tolerance and CPM-by-cohort pricing across personas.
cards.use_when: Planning or scaling a YouTube influencer program for a physical product brand, especially ones with broad audiences.

cards.title: Is Amazon or Google Shopping Under-Weighted in Your Mix?
cards.summary: Channel mix should reflect category demand capture, not a default 'Meta-first' assumption — Google Shopping and YouTube are still major drivers for certain categories.
cards.use_when: Reviewing channel allocation for a store whose category has clear search demand (jewelry, electronics, tools) but is over-indexed on Meta.

cards.title: Vivid Vision: Writing a Letter to Your Future Self as an Operator
cards.summary: Writing a dated letter from your future self clarifies what business and life outcomes you are actually building toward, which then guides strategy and risk-taking.
cards.use_when: Annual or multi-year planning for an ecommerce brand — choosing which markets, channels, or business models to build toward.

cards.title: Second-Mover Advantage in AI Adoption
cards.summary: The source argues for being a fast follower on AI tools — waiting to see what demonstrably moves profit before retooling teams around hype.
cards.use_when: Deciding how much resource to commit to AI tools and headcount for ecommerce operations, creative, and fulfillment.

cards.title: Automate influencer sourcing and outreach to scale partnership ads
cards.summary: Use AI to automate the find, screen, outreach and media-kit negotiation steps of influencer marketing so you can multiply conversations per week without adding headcount.
cards.use_when: Planning influencer/partnership ad acquisition and trying to increase creator volume for TikTok/Meta partnership ads.

cards.title: Back a human-first creative thesis while hedging on AI ads
cards.summary: The presenter bets platforms will reward real-human partnership ads over AI slop, but flags regulation and unclear platform incentives as real risks.
cards.use_when: Deciding how to allocate creative budget between human influencer/partnership ads and AI-generated statics/video.

cards.title: Localize pricing, language and merchandising to unlock non-US revenue
cards.summary: Model localization on a best-in-class case: per-market languages, localized pricing, and market-specific merchandising, not just one translated site.
cards.use_when: Expanding a DTC store into international markets or improving conversion in existing non-US traffic.

cards.title: Level 1 international shipping: one 3PL, one global campaign, best creatives
cards.summary: A simple first step for cross-border: house light inventory in a Hong Kong 3PL and run one Meta campaign with all best-performing North America creatives against every shippable country.
cards.use_when: Starting international expansion for a light-product store (e.g. phone cases, small electronics) with limited operational resources.

cards.title: Cross-border logistics can beat domestic fulfillment on cost and speed
cards.summary: A cross-border provider that dropships from Asia to US customers in under 5 days can be cheaper than domestic end-to-end fulfillment.
cards.use_when: Evaluating fulfillment options or trying to reduce shipping cost and delivery time for a US-facing store.

cards.title: Build a daily red/green/blue P&L report with mandatory explanations
cards.summary: Automate a daily Slack report of revenue, spend and key metrics with color status, and require the responsible owner to explain every miss in-thread.
cards.use_when: Setting up operating cadence and accountability for an ecommerce P&L.

cards.title: Run a daily task channel with every direct report
cards.summary: Each team member posts a morning plan and end-of-day completion plus time allocation, letting a leader spot overload and misplaced effort.
cards.use_when: Managing an ecommerce team's productivity and diagnosing why a channel (e.g. PPC) is missing targets.

cards.title: Reframe micromanagement as structured recurring feedback
cards.summary: The presenter says micromanagement fails only when it is unprompted, random and unstructured; make it predictable, daily and consistent to train juniors.
cards.use_when: Onboarding or developing junior ecommerce operators and deciding whether/how closely to manage them.

cards.title: Adopt the A Method's five-step hiring sequence
cards.summary: Scorecard, screening, topgrading, competency/culture, then reference-checked offer — a standardized sequence that made hiring comparable and durable.
cards.use_when: Building out an ecommerce team (e.g. head of finance or other key hires) and wanting a repeatable process to reduce early attrition.

cards.title: Write a role scorecard that separates outcomes from attributes
cards.summary: Define what the role must deliver and the specific competences/attributes needed, and explicitly list what does not matter to remove interviewer bias.
cards.use_when: Writing a job description or evaluating candidates for an ecommerce role (e.g. head of finance).

cards.title: Use screening booby-trap questions to test fit and flag deep-dive topics
cards.summary: A short standardized screen with deliberately probing questions surfaces fit and generates hypotheses to drill into during topgrading.
cards.use_when: Running first-round screens for any ecommerce role and deciding who advances.

cards.title: Topgrade candidates chronologically to find gaps and inflated titles
cards.summary: Walk every résumé role in order to verify what someone was actually hired to do versus their title, and to fill timeline gaps.
cards.use_when: Second-stage interviews where you need to verify a candidate's real track record before an ecommerce hire.

cards.title: Use case studies with traps plus a culture questionnaire
cards.summary: Test domain competence with a realistic exercise containing deliberate traps, then check cultural fit against your actual operating system.
cards.use_when: Final-stage evaluation of an ecommerce hire, especially specialized roles like finance or growth.

cards.title: Cut packaging cost and lift LTV with a bill of materials
cards.summary: Packaging spend hides in 'dummy numbers'; building a proper bill of materials exposes waste and packaging upgrades can raise LTV.
cards.use_when: Reviewing COGS/packaging for a DTC brand or sourcing better packaging suppliers.

cards.title: Automate procurement from weekly to daily purchase orders
cards.summary: At thousands of SKUs, custom software can move PO placement from weekly to daily with consistent logic, improving replenishment responsiveness.
cards.use_when: Managing replenishment and purchase orders for a high-SKU ecommerce catalog.

cards.title: Evaluate your business for picks-and-shovels spin-offs
cards.summary: Operators with proven internal capabilities (packaging, logistics, supply-chain software) can productize them for other brands as a new revenue line.
cards.use_when: Considering new revenue streams or evaluating whether an internal capability could serve other ecommerce brands.

cards.title: Check numbers daily, with a light weekend rule
cards.summary: Run the business like a bakery — count the buns and the cash every day — but consider explicitly pausing on weekends.
cards.use_when: Setting the leader's own operating rhythm for monitoring an ecommerce P&L.

cards.title: Topgrading interviews: chronological deep-dive by role
cards.summary: Run a topgrading interview that walks each résumé role chronologically and stress-tests title vs. actual scope, wins, lows, manager and exit reasons.
cards.use_when: Hiring for an ecommerce role with real budget or P&L impact — head of procurement, paid media buyer, supply chain lead, COO — where a wrong hire is expensive and résumé titles can inflate scope.

cards.title: Five-step funnel with a ~1% hiring acceptance rate
cards.summary: Structure hiring as scorecard, screening, topgrading, competency/culture and offer, and expect roughly 1% of applicants to receive an offer.
cards.use_when: Building a repeatable hiring pipeline for a growing ecommerce operation, or deciding how much screening effort a role justifies.

cards.title: Hire specialized roles in low-cost hubs, not US generalists
cards.summary: Salary arbitrage (roughly $100k US vs $20–30k Shenzhen vs ~$10k Philippines) works for specialized roles that need less cross-functional context.
cards.use_when: Choosing where to hire specialist procurement, paid-media or analytics staff for an ecommerce store.

cards.title: In-house vs agency: keep marketing in-house pre-$50M
cards.summary: If you're a sub-$50M brand, Roman argues you're winning on unique product or marketing savviness — so never outsource marketing if you're good at it.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to hand paid media, creative or growth to an agency versus building it in-house at a small-to-mid ecommerce brand.

cards.title: Fire C players without triggering A-player panic
cards.summary: Before mass layoffs, pre-brief your A players one-on-one so they don't read the cuts as a signal to leave.
cards.use_when: Cutting headcount or restructuring a store team, especially when layoffs are visible and top performers may interpret them as instability.

cards.title: Acquisition lens: only two levers — marketing spend and bill of materials
cards.summary: When evaluating a business to buy, ask where you have an unfair advantage in paid marketing spend or COGS renegotiation; a neglected ad account is a green field.
cards.use_when: Sourcing or underwriting an ecommerce acquisition, or deciding which existing store asset to buy into based on where you can add the most value.

cards.title: Founder red flags: avoid bad actors regardless of price
cards.summary: Roman's top acquisition filter is character: don't buy from — or sell to — someone you can't work with, even on great terms, because it never works out.
cards.use_when: Evaluating founders during acquisition talks, partnership discussions or supplier relationship decisions, especially when the numbers look attractive but people feel off.

cards.title: Use a five-slide recovery deck when negotiating to fix a bad hole
cards.summary: Roman's personal network deck to exit $3M in debt: acknowledge fault, explain the cause, state the plan, give a timeline and payback, then make the ask.
cards.use_when: Facing a serious cash shortfall in your ecommerce business — inventory overbuying, a failed product bet, or a debt hole — and needing capital or support from investors, partners or friends.

cards.title: Longevity as a category tailwind for the next decade
cards.summary: Roman's answer to 'what new brand would you launch tomorrow' is health and longevity, because he sees the cycle as still at the beginning.
cards.use_when: Choosing a category or new brand direction for an ecommerce product launch, or evaluating whether to double down on an existing health-adjacent line.

cards.title: Near-supplier location builds terms and iteration speed
cards.summary: Being geographically close to your manufacturer (e.g., Hong Kong for China sourcing) increases interaction frequency, which he argues speeds brand growth and unlocks better terms over time.
cards.use_when: Deciding where to base a China-reliant ecommerce operation, or planning supplier management visits and negotiation cadence for a product brand.

cards.title: Always be retaining, not just always be selling
cards.summary: Treat retention of top performers as a continuous discipline: pre-brief them on change, keep them informed before surprises, and never be blindsided by an A player resigning.
cards.use_when: Managing key ecommerce staff through growth, restructuring, budget cuts or channel pivots where uncertainty could push strong people out the door.

cards.title: When understaffed is the deliberate plan
cards.summary: Roman explicitly runs lean, near-zero excess capacity and hires only when seams show — a stated opex-first stance, not a universal default.
cards.use_when: Setting headcount and hiring plans for a lean ecommerce operation, especially when deciding whether to add roles ahead of demand.

cards.title: Keep Factories Aware of Backup Quotes to Preserve Leverage
cards.summary: Tell your factory you are actively quoting competitors and show them rival pricing; the source argues this strengthens rather than damages the relationship.
cards.use_when: An ecommerce seller is negotiating unit price, MOQ, or quality terms with a factory and wants to avoid being taken advantage of as a captive buyer.

cards.title: Write Exact Measurements in Spec Sheets, Never Vague Terms
cards.summary: Replace subjective descriptors like 'centered' in tech packs with precise dimensions so factories cannot make their own interpretation decisions.
cards.use_when: A seller is writing a tech pack, spec sheet, or decoration placement instructions for a factory before a production run.

cards.title: Use an authorized reference sample to specify store-product quality
cards.summary: When a client loves a product but finds it too expensive, send that physical sample to an overseas factory to replicate at lower cost.
cards.use_when: Qualifying a new manufacturer for a store-owned product or a design the brand is authorized to manufacture.

cards.title: Approve a new factory sample before committing to a store launch
cards.summary: Never pitch factory-sourced product to a buyer without first obtaining and inspecting a physical sample from that factory.
cards.use_when: Selecting a new supplier or product variation before placing a bulk purchase order for an ecommerce store.

cards.title: Diversify Sourcing Region by Trading Lead Time Against Cost
cards.summary: Choose manufacturing countries by weighing lead time, labor cost, raw-material origin and taxes rather than defaulting to China.
cards.use_when: A seller is choosing or relocating manufacturing for a product to reduce cost, shorten lead times, or reduce single-country supply chain risk.

cards.title: Maintain a vetted supplier shortlist by product category
cards.summary: The scarce part of sourcing isn't finding a factory but finding the best one, so build a curated factory library you can plug clients into.
cards.use_when: A seller or agency is deciding how to build a defensible sourcing advantage or differentiate from Alibaba-based competitors.

cards.title: Build a Tech Pack Before Contacting Any Factory
cards.summary: A tech pack is the product blueprint that stops factories from guessing on materials, colors, measurements and packaging, which is the root cause of inconsistent shipments.
cards.use_when: You are preparing to source a new physical product or reorder an existing one and need to lock specifications before requesting factory quotes.

cards.title: Shortlist and Vet Suppliers on Alibaba Before Committing
cards.summary: Treat Alibaba as a research tool: filter verified suppliers, message 10-15 factories, then verify with video calls and certification checks before shortlisting.
cards.use_when: You have a tech pack ready and need to find and screen candidate factories for a new product or a new category.

cards.title: Request a Structured Quote Before Sampling
cards.summary: A complete quote request forces suppliers to commit on unit cost, MOQ, lead time, packaging and payment terms so factories are comparable side by side.
cards.use_when: You have a shortlist of vetted factories and need comparable commercial terms to choose between them or use as negotiation leverage.

cards.title: Run the Sample Progression: Strike-Off to Pre-Production to Production
cards.summary: Advance through three sample stages and hold a factory sample as the gold standard reference so bulk orders can be checked against it.
cards.use_when: You are selecting between final candidate factories or preparing to green-light bulk production.

cards.title: Separate landed inventory cost from full delivered-order contribution
cards.summary: The supplier quote is only the X-factory price; landed cost adds freight, duties, taxes, insurance, warehousing, platform fees and 3PL pick/pack to reveal real per-unit profitability.
cards.use_when: You are deciding whether a product is viable, setting retail price, or evaluating a supplier quote before committing to a production run.

cards.title: Prioritize Flexibility Over Lowest Unit Cost in Early Production Runs
cards.summary: Chasing the cheapest unit price early can trap cash in unsold inventory; early runs are for learning velocity, quality consistency and delay patterns before negotiating hard.
cards.use_when: You are negotiating your first few production runs and deciding between a cheaper large order and a pricier smaller one.

cards.title: Choose Air vs Sea Freight with a Hybrid Strategy
cards.summary: Blend air freight for speed and sea freight for margin, choosing based on product size, weight and urgency rather than always taking the cheapest rate.
cards.use_when: You are planning how to move a finished production run from factory to warehouse.

cards.title: Book a Pre-Shipment QC Inspection Before the Container Leaves
cards.summary: A third-party QC inspection before shipment catches defects while the factory can still fix them; once goods are on the water, problems cannot be corrected.
cards.use_when: A production run is finishing at the factory and you are about to approve final payment and shipment.

cards.title: Select a 3PL with Documented Accuracy, Speed, Communication and Scalability
cards.summary: Fulfillment partners fail under peak volume; evaluate 3PLs on error rate, peak throughput, direct contacts and prior Q4 surge handling — and visit the warehouse.
cards.use_when: You are choosing or replacing a 3PL to store, pick, pack and ship orders, or evaluating whether your current one can handle forecast peak volume.

cards.title: Calculate Reorder Point with Velocity, Lead Time and Safety Stock
cards.summary: Reorder Point = (Daily Sales Velocity x Total Lead Time) + Safety Stock, so you reorder before running dry rather than chasing demand.
cards.use_when: You are setting reorder triggers and planning replenishment shipments for any SKU.

cards.title: Build a Weekly Forecasting Rhythm Even as a Solo Operator
cards.summary: Forecasting is not an afterthought: assign someone or a weekly ritual to review velocity, lead times and stock so demand spikes don't leave you sold out for months.
cards.use_when: You need a repeatable operating cadence to keep sourced products in stock and profitable, whether you are solo or have a small team.

cards.title: Keep Your Product Factory-Ready Before You Message Suppliers
cards.summary: Most sourcing problems start with the product definition, not the factory: unclear specs cause suppliers to guess, cut corners and produce inconsistent stock.
cards.use_when: You are defining a new product or fixing recurring inconsistency across reorders before you start supplier outreach.

cards.title: Protect IP and Build Long-Term Supplier Partnerships
cards.summary: Treat reliable suppliers as partners with early forecasts, on-time payment and repeat business, while keeping tech packs, artwork and source files on your side.
cards.use_when: You have selected a final supplier and are scaling volume, renewing terms, or assessing how much information to share.

cards.title: Use Volume Quotes to Reset Your Unit Cost Baseline
cards.summary: Post RFQs at multiple volume tiers to find how far per-unit cost falls, then weigh the discount against cash flow and defect risk.
cards.use_when: Product selection or replenishment: you are reordering a proven SKU and want to know whether moving from small Aliexpress-style batches to a bulk Alibaba order is worth the capital lock-up.

cards.title: Size defect allowances from observed quality instead of a fixed surplus
cards.summary: Use sample and batch defect evidence to plan usable stock while preventing defects through specifications and inspection.
cards.use_when: Purchase-order planning: you are placing or replenishing a bulk order and deciding the exact quantity to commit to.

cards.title: Test New Suppliers With Small Batches Before Switching
cards.summary: Run a cheaper supplier through a small test order while keeping your incumbent, and only migrate after verifying quality.
cards.use_when: Supplier negotiation or cost reduction: you've found a vendor quoting materially less and are tempted to move your whole order.

cards.title: Document order terms and pay through the protected Alibaba order route
cards.summary: Route supplier payments through Alibaba's built-in gateway for buyer protection rather than direct transfers.
cards.use_when: Supplier payment: you are about to send a deposit or balance to a Chinese supplier and choosing the payment method.

cards.title: Get a Direct Messaging Channel to Avoid Supplier Ghosting
cards.summary: Collect the supplier's WhatsApp, WeChat or email early so an offline Alibaba chat thread doesn't stall your order.
cards.use_when: Supplier communication during quoting, sampling, production or shipping: you need reliable contact to confirm specs, defects or shipment timing.

cards.title: Match Shipping Method to Item Weight and Deadline
cards.summary: Choose sea freight, air cargo, or premium courier based on item weight and how far ahead of peak season you order.
cards.use_when: Fulfillment planning and replenishment timing: you are ordering heavy or bulky products and deciding how they get to your warehouse.

cards.title: Negotiate Down Per-Unit Cost Before You Commit Volume
cards.summary: Ask suppliers for a lower unit price rather than accepting the initial quote; small per-unit reductions compound across a large order.
cards.use_when: Supplier negotiation: you have a quote in hand for a replenishment or new-product bulk order and are deciding whether to push back on price.

cards.title: Use Sourcing Agents Deliberately and Vet Them
cards.summary: Sourcing agents can unlock manufacturer access, customisation and better pricing, but require diligence on who you choose.
cards.use_when: Product selection and sourcing strategy: you need customisation, factory-direct access, or better prices than trading-company quotes on Alibaba.

cards.title: Structure Bulk Purchases Around Cash Flow, Not Just Unit Price
cards.summary: Unused volume and freight discounts can be leveraged through payment or inventory structures rather than taken as straight price cuts.
cards.use_when: Replenishment and cash-flow planning: you are ordering a recurring SKU several times a year and weighing a larger order tier against working capital.

cards.title: Do unscalable retention interventions on a narrow VIP segment
cards.summary: Apply Paul Graham's 'do things that don't scale' to ecommerce by manually over-serving a narrow set of customers to prove the value hypothesis before automating.
cards.use_when: You are deciding whether to invest in automated CRM flows or manual high-touch interventions for a new or high-LTV customer segment, or validating a premium offer before scaling spend.

cards.title: Send unbranded artifacts instead of logo swag
cards.summary: Giftology's core rule: give high-quality, unbranded 'artifacts' the recipient would want to own, never logo-driven promotional swag.
cards.use_when: You are selecting a thank-you or retention gift for top customers, VIP buyers or wholesale/B2B accounts and deciding what to send.

cards.title: Time retention gifts to unexpected, random moments
cards.summary: Deliver gifts on random dates (a random Tuesday in April) rather than holidays or purchase anniversaries, which dilute the emotional impact.
cards.use_when: You are scheduling surprise gifts, handwritten notes or delight moments for high-value customers and picking the send date.

cards.title: Test an optional household gift for high-value ecommerce customers
cards.summary: Expand radical generosity beyond the primary buyer to spouses, children or assistants to recruit internal advocates who lock in loyalty.
cards.use_when: Designing a small VIP gifting test where customers have voluntarily expressed an appropriate household gifting preference.

cards.title: Empower frontline agents to make micro-personalized wild bets
cards.summary: Guidara's 'unreasonable hospitality' translated to ecommerce: give support or warehouse staff a discretionary budget to send hyper-specific gifts based on zero-party data from conversations.
cards.use_when: You are setting support or fulfillment policy and deciding whether agents may act on customer details shared during routine interactions.

cards.title: Respond sensitively when a subscriber voluntarily shares hardship
cards.summary: Chewy's empathic operations wild bet: flag sudden long-term subscription cancellations, refund without returns, and send physical gestures when a customer suffers a loss.
cards.use_when: You operate subscriptions/auto-replenishment and are defining cancellation and cancellation-reason workflows for consumable or pet/family products.

cards.title: Use pet portraits as an unfair content and referral engine
cards.summary: Chewy's hand-painted surprise pet portraits show that a costly, unscalable gift can generate high-converting user-generated content and referrals.
cards.use_when: You are considering a signature high-cost surprise gift as a brand differentiation and acquisition flywheel.

cards.title: Resolve failures effortlessly before attempting to delight
cards.summary: Dixon's Effortless Experience research (97,000+ interactions) shows delight does not create loyalty during service failures — eliminating effort does.
cards.use_when: You are deciding how customer support should handle shipping delays, broken items, billing errors and returns, and whether to attach freebies or discounts to those interactions.

cards.title: Map wild bets vs effortless operations to the right touchpoint
cards.summary: Split retention strategy: ruthlessly reduce friction on routine and failure touchpoints, deploy unscalable delight only on high-LTV cohorts in neutral or positive states.
cards.use_when: You are allocating retention budget and deciding which touchpoints get delight gifts versus process simplification.

cards.title: Design anti-marketing stunts that polarize and filter
cards.summary: Cards Against Humanity's Black Friday stunts show that absurd, anti-consumerist campaigns can generate oversized earned media and a tribal community — at the cost of exclusivity.
cards.use_when: You are planning a campaign for a brand targeting Millennials/Gen Z or in a commoditized category where paid media is too expensive to win.

cards.title: Fix real pain points in the physical product; drop marketing gimmicks
cards.summary: Mokobara won a commoditized luggage category by investing in premium Japanese Hinomoto wheels and a practical laptop pocket while rejecting USB charging gimmicks that fail in real use.
cards.use_when: You are making product development or vendor selection decisions and choosing between features that market well and features that solve real customer complaints.

cards.title: Distribute through unexpected channels and integrations
cards.summary: Mokobara bypassed crowded marketplaces by being the exclusive premium luggage brand on a 10-minute quick-commerce app and pairing with an airline for real utility.
cards.use_when: You are planning channel expansion and looking for share-of-voice niches that avoid Amazon/Flipkart ad competition.

cards.title: Capture zero-party data before offering the discount
cards.summary: Use a multi-step quiz or segmentation pop-up before the incentive so acquisition collects personalization data instead of attracting low-intent bargain hunters.
cards.use_when: You are designing a pop-up, quiz funnel or landing page at the top of the funnel and deciding whether to lead with the discount.

cards.title: Run a Proactive Pause email to prevent subscription churn
cards.summary: Monitor usage data and proactively email overloaded customers to pause their subscription, trading short-term revenue for permanent trust.
cards.use_when: You run a replenishment or subscription program and have data showing shipment cadence versus consumption.

cards.title: Treat paid loyalty programs as a retention lever
cards.summary: Source-reported McKinsey data indicate paid loyalty members are 60% more likely to increase spending — twice the likelihood of free-program members.
cards.use_when: You are designing a loyalty program or tier structure and deciding between free points-based and paid/exclusive access models.

cards.title: Build direct community engagement, not broadcast channels
cards.summary: Retention moats come from cultivating community through interactive content and personalized engagement, not from broadcasting offers to followers.
cards.use_when: You are planning social media and content operations and deciding whether to invest in community interactions or paid reach.

cards.title: Own the first 100 days with an eight-phase onboarding journey
cards.summary: Joey Coleman's framework: churn concentrates in the first 100 days, so sequence mailers, videos and upgrades to replace buyer's remorse with anticipation.
cards.use_when: You are designing the post-purchase experience and deciding what to send and when between purchase and first repeat order.

cards.title: Systematically run manual letters to top repeat buyers
cards.summary: The Founder's Ink tactic: annually handwrite customized letters to the top 1% of repeat buyers referencing specific past purchases, with no discount codes.
cards.use_when: You are planning a high-touch retention gesture for your best customers and debating whether to include an incentive.
